name: Node maintenance: taint, drain, uncordon, label
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Maintenance & Troubleshooting. Drill EVERY node-level cluster-ops corner harder than the exam: static pods and mirror pods, repairing a crash-looping control-plane component, etcd snapshot backup, node taints and labels, cordon/drain for maintenance, uncordon to return a node, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state via docker exec and kubectl -o json.

questions.title: Taint a node (NoSchedule)
questions.teach:
A **taint** repels pods lacking a matching **toleration**: `kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:effect`. `NoSchedule` blocks new pods that don't tolerate it; it is recorded in the node's `spec.taints`.

**Gotcha:** a taint only affects *scheduling* of new pods — it does NOT evict already-running pods (that behavior is `NoExecute`).
questions.prompt:
Taint worker node `$W1` so ordinary pods won't schedule there: key `workload`, value `batch`, effect `NoSchedule`.

Target: `$W1` has a taint `workload=batch:NoSchedule` in `spec.taints`.
questions.hint: `kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule`. Inspect with `kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'`.
questions.eli5:
A **taint** is a "Keep Out" sign you hang on a node. By default, every pod reads the sign and stays away. A pod can only land there if it carries a matching **toleration** — a little pass that says "I'm allowed past this exact sign."

Think of the node as a reserved meeting room. Running `kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule` hangs a sign on the room that reads `workload=batch`, with strength `NoSchedule`. From now on, the scheduler won't put *new* pods in that room unless they explicitly tolerate `workload=batch`.

A taint has three parts: a **key** (`workload`), a **value** (`batch`), and an **effect** (`NoSchedule`). The effect is how strict the sign is. `NoSchedule` means "no new guests without a pass" — but importantly, anyone already sitting in the room gets to stay. It only affects *future* scheduling decisions.

**Watch out:**

- **A `NoSchedule` taint does NOT evict pods already running** on the node. Only the `NoExecute` effect kicks out existing pods. If you expected the node to empty and it didn't, that's why — use `drain` (next step) or `NoExecute` for that.
- The taint is stored in the node's `spec.taints`, not in its labels. Check it with `kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'`.
- A taint only **repels**; it never **attracts**. Giving a pod the matching toleration just *permits* it onto the node — it doesn't force it there.
- To **remove** a taint, repeat the command with a trailing dash: `kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule-`.
questions.deepDive:
## Tainting a node (NoSchedule) — full rundown

### Mental model
**Taints repel. Tolerations permit.** A taint lives on the **node** (`spec.taints`) and keeps pods off unless each pod carries a matching **toleration**. A taint is three parts: `key=value:effect`.

```bash
kubectl taint nodes <node> workload=batch:NoSchedule
#                          └ key ┘ └value┘ └ effect ┘
```

### The three effects
| Effect | New pods without a toleration | Already-running pods without a toleration |
|---|---|---|
| **NoSchedule** | ❌ not scheduled here | ✅ stay (untouched) |
| **PreferNoSchedule** | ⚠️ avoided if possible, else allowed | ✅ stay |
| **NoExecute** | ❌ not scheduled here | ❌ **evicted** |

Only `NoExecute` touches running pods. This step uses `NoSchedule`, so existing pods are left in place.

### Managing taints
```bash
# add
kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule

# change an existing taint's effect/value (same key) — needs --overwrite
kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule --overwrite

# REMOVE — trailing dash, and the effect must match
kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule-

# inspect
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'; echo
kubectl describe node $W1 | grep -A2 Taints
```
- `value` is optional: `kubectl taint nodes $W1 dedicated:NoSchedule` (key-only taint).
- A node may hold **many** taints; a pod must tolerate **every** applicable taint to schedule there.

### Matching toleration (on the pod, for reference)
```yaml
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: workload
    operator: Equal        # Equal (default) | Exists
    value: batch           # only with operator: Equal
    effect: NoSchedule     # match a specific effect, or omit to tolerate all effects of this key
```

### Well-known / built-in taints
| Taint | When | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` | control-plane nodes | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` | node not Ready | `NoExecute` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` | node controller lost contact | `NoExecute` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable` | node cordoned | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` / `disk-pressure` / `pid-pressure` | resource pressure | `NoSchedule` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`NoSchedule` does not evict running pods** — a very common trap. Use `NoExecute`, or `kubectl drain`, to clear a node.
- Taints go in **`spec.taints`**, not `metadata.labels`. Don't confuse tainting with labelling.
- **Removing** a taint needs the trailing `-` *and* the matching `effect` (`workload=batch:NoSchedule-`).
- A toleration **permits but does not attract** — pair with `nodeSelector`/affinity to force placement.
- Changing an existing taint in place requires `--overwrite`; otherwise `kubectl` errors that the taint already exists.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule          # add
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'; echo     # verify
kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule-          # remove (trailing dash)
```

questions.title: Cordon and drain a node
questions.teach:
To prep a node for maintenance, `kubectl cordon` sets `spec.unschedulable=true` (no *new* pods); `kubectl drain` then evicts existing pods (and cordons automatically). Pass `--ignore-daemonsets` and `--delete-emptydir-data`.

**Gotcha:** without those two flags, drain refuses — read the error, add the flag, rerun.
questions.prompt:
Node `$W2` needs maintenance. Cordon it, then drain it (ignoring DaemonSets and deleting emptyDir data).

Target: `$W2` is cordoned — `spec.unschedulable=true` — and the drain completed.
questions.eli5:
Imagine a node is a bus, and the pods on it are passengers. You need to take the bus to the garage for maintenance. Two steps make that safe.

**Cordon** is putting an "Out of Service" sign in the bus window. New passengers can't board (`kubectl cordon` sets `spec.unschedulable=true`), but anyone already riding stays put for now.

**Drain** is actually clearing the bus: it politely asks each passenger to get off (evicts the pods) so the controllers can re-seat them on other buses, and it automatically puts up the "Out of Service" sign too (drain cordons for you). Once drain finishes, the node is empty of ordinary workloads and safe to work on.

The one twist: a few passengers are *staff* — things like the CNI/network agent and `kube-proxy`, which ride every bus as a **DaemonSet**. Drain won't evict those unless you say so, and it refuses to proceed until you acknowledge them.

**Watch out:**

- **Drain refuses by default** when DaemonSet pods or pods using `emptyDir` are present. Read the error, then add `--ignore-daemonsets` and `--delete-emptydir-data` and rerun. (`emptyDir` data is **lost** — that's the point of the flag.)
- Drain **cordons automatically** — you don't strictly need a separate `cordon` first, but doing it is harmless and idempotent.
- Standalone pods not backed by a controller block drain too; use `--force` to delete them (they won't come back elsewhere).
- Draining respects **PodDisruptionBudgets** — if a PDB won't allow the eviction, drain waits. Use `--timeout` to bound the wait.
questions.deepDive:
## Cordon & drain a node — full rundown

### Mental model
Preparing a node for maintenance is two actions:
- **`cordon`** — mark the node **unschedulable** (`spec.unschedulable=true`). No *new* pods land; existing pods keep running.
- **`drain`** — **evict** the existing pods (so controllers reschedule them elsewhere) **and** cordon the node automatically.

`cordon` + `uncordon` just flip a boolean. `drain` does the real eviction work.

### Commands
```bash
kubectl cordon $W2                         # spec.unschedulable=true, nothing evicted

kubectl drain $W2 \
  --ignore-daemonsets \                    # don't block on DaemonSet pods (they can't be rescheduled)
  --delete-emptydir-data                   # allow evicting pods with emptyDir volumes (data is LOST)

# other useful flags:
#   --force                 delete pods not managed by a controller (bare pods)
#   --grace-period=30       override pod termination grace period
#   --timeout=120s          give up waiting after this long
#   --pod-selector=app=x    only drain matching pods
#   --dry-run=client        preview what would be evicted
```

### Why those flags
| Situation | Default drain behavior | Flag that fixes it |
|---|---|---|
| DaemonSet-managed pods present | **refuses** (they'd just be recreated on the same node) | `--ignore-daemonsets` |
| Pods with `emptyDir` volumes | **refuses** (data would be lost) | `--delete-emptydir-data` |
| Bare pods (no controller) | **refuses** (nothing would recreate them) | `--force` |
| A PodDisruptionBudget blocks eviction | **waits/errors** | fix PDB or `--timeout` |

Read the error — drain tells you exactly which condition stopped it, and which flag to add.

### What drain does under the hood
It uses the **Eviction API** (`/eviction` subresource), which honors **PodDisruptionBudgets**. DaemonSet pods are skipped (with `--ignore-daemonsets`); mirror/static pods are never evicted. After draining, `kubectl get node` shows `SchedulingDisabled`.

### cordon vs drain vs taint
| Action | Effect on new pods | Effect on running pods | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cordon` | blocked | untouched | `spec.unschedulable=true` |
| `drain` | blocked (auto-cordons) | **evicted** | eviction API |
| taint `NoSchedule` | blocked (if untolerated) | untouched | `spec.taints` |
| taint `NoExecute` | blocked | **evicted** | `spec.taints` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Drain without the two flags fails** on most real nodes — the error names the blocker; add `--ignore-daemonsets` and `--delete-emptydir-data` and rerun. This is the classic exam moment.
- `--delete-emptydir-data` **destroys** that pod's emptyDir contents — expected for maintenance, but know it.
- Drain **auto-cordons**; a separate `cordon` first is optional and idempotent.
- `drain` does **not** remove the node from the cluster — it only empties it. The node is still registered and `Ready`, just `SchedulingDisabled`.
- Evicted pods restart elsewhere **only if a controller owns them** (Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet/DaemonSet). Bare pods removed with `--force` are gone for good.
- After maintenance, you must **`uncordon`** to let the scheduler use the node again.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl cordon $W2
kubectl drain  $W2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl get node $W2            # STATUS shows Ready,SchedulingDisabled
# ... do maintenance ...
kubectl uncordon $W2            # return to service
```

questions.title: Uncordon the control-plane
questions.teach:
`kubectl uncordon <node>` reverses a cordon, setting `spec.unschedulable=false` to return the node to service. It does **not** pull back pods that drain evicted — the scheduler places *new* pods there over time.

**Gotcha:** `uncordon` takes a **node** name (not a pod) and is idempotent — running it on a schedulable node is a no-op.
questions.prompt:
The control-plane node `$CP` was cordoned for maintenance. Bring it back into service.

Target: `$CP` is schedulable again — `spec.unschedulable` is not `true`.
questions.eli5:
Remember the "Out of Service" sign from cordon/drain? **Uncordon** is simply taking that sign back down.

When maintenance on a node is finished, `kubectl uncordon <node>` flips the node back to **schedulable** — it sets `spec.unschedulable` back to `false`. The node rejoins the pool of places the scheduler is willing to use, and over time new pods start landing there again.

Here the node happens to be the **control-plane** node `$CP`, which was cordoned for maintenance. Uncordoning it is exactly the same one-liner as for any worker: `kubectl uncordon $CP`.

The one thing people expect but *don't* get: uncordon does **not** pull back the pods that `drain` evicted earlier. Those pods already found new homes and stay there. Uncordon only makes the node **eligible** again for *future* scheduling decisions — it refills gradually and naturally, not instantly.

**Watch out:**

- **Uncordon takes a NODE name, not a pod name.** It's a node-level operation.
- It's **idempotent** — running it on a node that's already schedulable does nothing and is not an error. Safe to run twice.
- It **won't re-attract** the drained pods. The node fills back up only as the scheduler places new work.
- Confirm success with `kubectl get node $CP` — the `STATUS` column should no longer say `SchedulingDisabled`.
- Note the control-plane node may still carry its built-in `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule` **taint**, which is separate from cordoning — uncordon doesn't touch taints.
questions.deepDive:
## Uncordon a node — full rundown

### Mental model
`uncordon` is the inverse of `cordon`: it clears **`spec.unschedulable`** (sets it to `false`), returning the node to the pool the scheduler will place new pods on. It does **not** move any pods — it only changes future scheduling eligibility.

```bash
kubectl uncordon $CP
kubectl get node $CP          # STATUS no longer shows SchedulingDisabled
```

### The maintenance lifecycle
| Phase | Command | `spec.unschedulable` | Pods |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prep | `kubectl cordon $N` | `true` | existing stay |
| Evacuate | `kubectl drain $N …` | `true` (auto) | evicted/rescheduled |
| Maintenance | — | `true` | node empty of normal pods |
| Return | `kubectl uncordon $N` | `false` | scheduler may place NEW pods |

### What uncordon does and does not do
- ✅ Sets `spec.unschedulable=false` so the scheduler considers the node again.
- ❌ Does **not** pull back pods that drain evicted — they stay where they were rescheduled.
- ❌ Does **not** remove **taints**. Cordon/uncordon toggles a boolean; taints are a separate list in `spec.taints`. A control-plane node keeps its `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule` taint regardless.
- ✅ Is **idempotent** — uncordoning an already-schedulable node is a harmless no-op.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get node $CP
# NAME   STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
# $CP    Ready    control-plane   7d    v1.3x.x     <- no "SchedulingDisabled"

kubectl get node $CP -o jsonpath='{.spec.unschedulable}'; echo   # empty or false
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **It takes a node name, not a pod name** — `kubectl uncordon <node>`.
- `cordon`/`uncordon` only flip `unschedulable`; they are **not** taints. If pods still won't land after uncordon, check `spec.taints` and pod tolerations separately.
- Uncordon alone doesn't "rebalance" the cluster — the drained node refills only as new pods are scheduled.
- Idempotent: re-running it won't error, so it's safe in scripts.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl uncordon $CP                                  # back to service
kubectl get node $CP                                   # confirm no SchedulingDisabled
kubectl get node $CP -o jsonpath='{.spec.unschedulable}'; echo
```

questions.title: Label a node
questions.teach:
Node **labels** are `key=value` metadata used by `nodeSelector`/affinity to steer scheduling. Add one with `kubectl label node <node> key=value`; replace an existing key with `--overwrite`.

**Gotcha:** labels (`metadata.labels`, for selection) are NOT taints (`spec.taints`, for repelling) — this step wants a label.
questions.prompt:
Label worker node `$W2` with `disk=ssd` so a storage workload can target it.

Target: `$W2` has label `disk=ssd` in `metadata.labels`.
questions.hint: `kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd`. Check with `kubectl get node $W2 --show-labels` or `-o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.disk}'`.
questions.eli5:
A node **label** is just a sticky note you attach to a node: a `key=value` tag that describes something about it — like `disk=ssd`, `zone=east`, or `gpu=true`. Labels don't *do* anything by themselves; they're how you *describe* nodes so that pods can later say "put me somewhere with that note."

Here you tag worker `$W2` with `disk=ssd` using `kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd`. Later, a storage-hungry pod can use a `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` of `disk=ssd` to steer itself onto this node.

The key thing to keep straight: a **label attracts**, a **taint repels** — they're opposites and they live in different places. A label is friendly metadata in `metadata.labels` that pods *select*. A taint is a "keep out" entry in `spec.taints` that pushes pods *away*. This step wants a **label**, so use `kubectl label`, not `kubectl taint`.

**Watch out:**

- **Don't confuse labels with taints.** Label = `metadata.labels` (for selecting/attracting). Taint = `spec.taints` (for repelling). This step wants the label.
- If the key **already exists** with a different value, plain `kubectl label` fails with "already has a value." Add `--overwrite` to replace it.
- To **remove** a label, use a trailing dash: `kubectl label node $W2 disk-`.
- A label alone doesn't move any pods — it only matters once a pod's `nodeSelector`/affinity references it.
- Check it with `kubectl get node $W2 --show-labels` or `-o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.disk}'`.
questions.deepDive:
## Labelling a node — full rundown

### Mental model
A **label** is `key=value` metadata in a node's `metadata.labels`. Labels **attract**: pods reference them via `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` to steer scheduling. Labels are the opposite of **taints** (which repel and live in `spec.taints`).

### Commands
```bash
# add a label
kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd

# replace an existing key's value (plain label fails if the key already exists)
kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd --overwrite

# remove a label (trailing dash)
kubectl label node $W2 disk-

# inspect
kubectl get node $W2 --show-labels
kubectl get nodes -L disk                               # 'disk' as its own column
kubectl get node $W2 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.disk}'; echo
```

### How a pod uses the label
```yaml
spec:
  nodeSelector:            # hard requirement, exact key=value
    disk: ssd
```
or richer matching via affinity:
```yaml
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
          - { key: disk, operator: In, values: [ssd, nvme] }
```

### Label vs taint — don't mix them up
| | Label | Taint |
|---|---|---|
| Stored in | `metadata.labels` | `spec.taints` |
| Purpose | **attract** (pods select it) | **repel** (pods avoid unless tolerating) |
| Command | `kubectl label node …` | `kubectl taint nodes …` |
| Pod side | `nodeSelector` / `nodeAffinity` | `tolerations` |

### Built-in node labels (already present, selectable)
| Label | Example |
|---|---|
| `kubernetes.io/hostname` | the node name |
| `kubernetes.io/os` | `linux` / `windows` |
| `kubernetes.io/arch` | `amd64` / `arm64` |
| `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` | on control-plane nodes |
| `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` / `region` | cloud topology |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Label ≠ taint.** The most common mix-up: `kubectl label` adds attracting metadata; `kubectl taint` adds repelling entries. Read the task wording carefully.
- Re-labelling an existing key **requires `--overwrite`**, or `kubectl` errors `node/... already has a value (...) for key ...`.
- A label **does nothing on its own** — it only affects scheduling once a pod's `nodeSelector`/affinity references it.
- Label keys may be prefixed (`example.com/team=a`); the `node-restriction.kubernetes.io/` prefix is special (kubelets can't self-set it). Plain keys like `disk=ssd` are fine.
- Removing a label (trailing `-`) can strand pods that selected it on the next (re)schedule.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd --overwrite             # add/replace
kubectl get node $W2 --show-labels                       # verify
kubectl label node $W2 disk-                             # remove
```
